questions.question: A test has 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity; prevalence is 1%. P(disease | positive) ≈ ?
A p-value is:
options: The probability the null hypothesis is true
The probability the result will replicate
The probability of observing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true

questions.question: Checking an A/B test daily and stopping at the first p < 0.05:
options: Has no effect on error rates
Inflates the false-positive rate; use a fixed horizon or sequential testing
questions.explanation: Each peek is another chance to cross the threshold by luck.

questions.question: Expected number of fair coin flips to get two heads in a row?
questions.explanation: Solve E = ½(1 + E) + ¼(2 + E) + ¼·2 → E = 6.

questions.question: Monty Hall: should you switch?
options: Only if the host chooses randomly
questions.explanation: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time; the host's informed reveal concentrates the remaining 2/3 on the other door.

questions.question: Uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length:
options: Store everything and sample at the end
Reservoir sampling: keep item i with probability k/i, replacing a random reservoir slot
questions.explanation: One pass, O(k) memory, exactly uniform.

questions.question: The Central Limit Theorem says the sample mean of many i.i.d. variables with finite variance is approximately:
options: Normal with mean μ and variance σ²/n

questions.question: Poisson(λ) has mean and variance:
questions.explanation: Overdispersion (variance > mean) in count data suggests a negative binomial.

questions.question: Unbiased sample variance divides by n − 1 because:
options: Variance is always overestimated by n
The sample mean is estimated from the same data, using up one degree of freedom
It makes the variance larger for safety

questions.question: Minimizing MSE in linear regression is equivalent to maximum likelihood under:
questions.explanation: Laplace noise ↔ MAE; Bernoulli ↔ cross-entropy (logistic regression).

questions.question: Testing 20 independent metrics at α = 0.05 with no real effects, expected false positives?
Simpson's paradox is:
options: A trend in every subgroup that reverses when the groups are combined
questions.explanation: Caused by a confounder that affects group sizes; segment your analysis.

questions.question: Halving the minimum detectable effect in an A/B test requires roughly how much more sample?
Generate a fair bit from a biased coin.
questions.answer: Flip twice: HT → 0, TH → 1, HH or TT → discard and repeat (von Neumann). Works because P(HT) = P(TH) = p(1−p).

questions.question: Explain a 95% confidence interval correctly.
questions.answer: If you repeated the experiment many times and built an interval each time, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true parameter. It's not a 95% probability that this specific interval contains it (that's a Bayesian credible interval).

questions.question: Type I vs type II error, and power?
questions.answer: Type I: false positive (rejecting a true null), rate α. Type II: false negative (missing a real effect), rate β. Power = 1 − β, usually targeted at 0.8.

questions.question: Birthday problem answer for 23 people?
questions.answer: ≈ 50.7% chance at least two share a birthday. Compute 1 − Π(365−i)/365 for i = 0..22.
